231.t: Fighting off white kids who stoned black schoolchildren
231.s: He sets up piles of rocks behind a tree and drives off white boys who throw rocks at black children on the way home; the goat is later sold.
231.q: in the school. Then I wanted to be at the head of the class in singing. I wanted to be at the head of the class in drawing, manual training, all this, / I wanted to be at the head of the class, so I worked hard at that and worked hard at that. So finally -- we were coming home from school and all…

231.t: The park swing confrontation and his name Bubber
231.s: Barred from the chain swings, he refuses to leave one; he explains his boyhood name Bubber Sublette and escapes a gang of boys.
231.q: Then I wanted to go to a park in Indianapolis where they have lawn swings and they have chain swings, but they didn't allow colored people to walk children to swing on the swings, chain swings, you know. But you could swing on the lawn swings, you know, old lawn swings with backs to them that four…

231.t: Why the Detention Home decision mattered: prejudice and violence
231.s: He argues leaving Indianapolis put him in line for bigger stages and thanks the Judge, saying he would have killed someone as a man.
231.ch: Louisville, Buck and the carnival years
231.q: Getting me out of the Detention Home and being able to participate in the Amateur Night thing, that put me in the line of professional. I got to go farther than where I am. And where can I go? It's just like here, where can you go after you play the Orpheum Theatre. Got to go to San Francisco,…

231.s: As the only Negro paper boy, he was made to box another boy and earned respect.
231.ch: Brawls, the Ink Spots and boyhood recollections
231.q: During the time I was in Indianapolis when I was selling papers like the Indianapolis Star and the baseball extras, I used to have to go to the newspaper office to get my papers. So I'd get to the paper office to get my papers, quite a few of the boys -- me being the only negro boy seemed like was…

231.t: Cutting a boy and running from the mob
231.s: He opens a pocket knife on the crowd and cuts one boy, then flees home and over fences, hiding behind a piano box.
231.q: So I guess about eight or nine of the boys run and one fella stood there. He's the one fella that got cut. So when I cut him, that was all. Soon as I saw the blood, that was all, and I turned and I run. They ran me all the way up to my house, I was right across from the park, they run me in there.…

417.t: The Bensons' street reputation and his cousin's death in a gang fight
417.s: He describes his tough cousins, how one was killed, and the fight at the Fifth Avenue basketball court.
417.q: knew they were going to have to go through crazy Benson, Tommy the Mule, because they say when they got hit by Tommy, it was like being kicked with a mule, and they called him Shotgun. One guy said it was like being hit with a shotgun blast. So they called him Shotgun and Mule. So, if you was a…

417.t: Friend Sylvester 'Poopado' Harring and the little toughies
417.s: He describes a muscular friend who picked fights for him and how their group earned respect.
417.q: The hurting part was, I could outrun anybody, out-swim anybody. And I had a friend who was better than me. He was black also. He was crazy, though. He’d do 200 pushups like it wasn’t nothing, like nothing. Nobody could even get close to him. He was built like Superman. He was my same size, but he…

703.t: The Robinson brothers' roller-skating speeding ticket
703.s: Tells the legend of Jackie and Mack Robinson being ticketed for skating to Huntington Beach and the town's celebration.
703.q: There were three boys, Mack, Jackie, and Elroy. Elroy was the troublemaker. He was always in a bunch of trouble, getting in a bunch of trouble, because – I guess just because of the pressure of having these other two brothers who were something. One of the most famous stories about the Robinsons is…

503.t: Black Bottom violence and how music kept him out of gangs
503.s: Growing up amid fights and gangs, he says music changed his outlook and protected him.
503.ch: High school, Dizzy and Wayne State
503.q: I’d say maybe twenty, that’s a big area and that was the area that both my grade school and high school were in and it was not an easy place to grow up because there was a lot of fights, you know, a lot of violence. But at the same time I learned to get along with people and one of the main things…

111.s: He describes a mixed neighborhood of many languages where neighbors helped each other and the schools were integrated.
111.q: to plow. We had a couple acres of land where we’d plant our garden so I always enjoyed seeing things like that. My father was so—he knew everybody. He didn’t have any bad feelings about him at all. And people do favors for him, he’d do favors for them, it was back and forth. People need a cup of…

373.t: Roxbury, Boston anti-Semitism and growing up an outsider
373.s: He describes his mostly Jewish Roxbury neighborhood, Father Coughlin, street danger and the Muggsy Spanier record story.
373.q: Yeah. Roxbury was interestingly divided. It was mostly Jewish. When Franklin D. Roosevelt was running, and I thought he was the permanent President, he carried our ward, Ward 12, overwhelmingly, but we also had some communists and anarchists. I think the latter were non-violent. But the communists…

509.t: Growing up in Woodridge and whether race mattered
509.s: She describes the working-class Woodridge neighborhood and her family nearby; she recalls no racial awareness, mentioning Aunt Cleo in St. Louis.
509.q: Well, you know, there was a difference here. There‘s ten years‘ difference between my brother, my oldest brother and me, you know. Ask that question again.

386.t: Forged writs of habeas corpus for black kids in jail
386.s: He tells how he freed Black kids from Dallas jails with writs signed by a judge.
386.q: One of the things I used to do...in Dallas they had a thing called...they had two jails, the city jail and the county jail. If you were in the city jail, arrested for something, and they transferred you to the county jail, after they filed charges against you...well, they had a thing called a writ…

31.t: Boxers Sam Langford, Jack Johnson and Henry Armstrong
31.s: He never met Jack Johnson, but was a buddy of fighter Sam Langford and recalls Gunboat Smith and Henry Armstrong watching him play.
31.q: Jack Johnson? Jack Johnson I never met, but he was -- up in 1914, he was up there in Chelsea, Massachusetts. But I didn't see him, see. And I think Sam Langford -- see, I used to be a buddy of Sam Langford's.

75.t: 63rd Street neighbors: Benny Carter's father and Russell Procope
75.s: He recalls Benny Carter, Russell Procope and others on 63rd Street, a knife fight by Benny's father, and Procope as the first person he saw play piano.
75.ch: Teens, stride pianists and the Louisiana Stompers
75.q: Benny Carter's father was there. I saw Benny Carter's father cut a man's ear from here to here. You know? The guy had hit him, and he came down and he cut that man. But don't say it... I saw him later, a year before he died, and he said, 'Son, how you been?' He didn't even know that I... Because…

125.t: Becoming physical at twelve: defending his violin in new neighborhoods
125.s: He describes fending off bullies who wanted his violin or bicycle in semi-integrated neighborhoods, and how his father taught him to avoid fights.
125.q: Well, I -- for some reason or other that's why I play so much importance on age 12 in my life. It's because this was when I started everything. Athletics and everything.
